identification.name: Beryllium (Structural Grade S-65)
identification.common_form_notes: Produced by hot isostatic pressing (HIP) of beryllium powder; supplied as billets, plates, and near-net forgings by specialist suppliers (Materion Corp). CRITICAL: all machining must be performed under strict industrial hygiene controls — see Notes.
identification.notes: HEALTH WARNING — CONFIRMED HUMAN CARCINOGEN. Inhalation of beryllium dust or fumes causes chronic beryllium disease (CBD), a severe and irreversible lung condition. All machining, grinding, or abrading must be performed under wet conditions with HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air)-filtered enclosures and supplied-air respiratory protection per OSHA (Occupational Safety and Health Administration) 29 CFR (Code of Federal Regulations) 1910.1024. Beryllium sensitisation can occur at very low exposures (PEL, permissible exposure limit: 0.2 µg/m³ TWA (time-weighted average)). Finished, non-abraded parts present minimal risk. Consult your institution's occupational health and safety office before handling any machined beryllium. S-65 grade designation by Materion Corp (formerly Brush Wellman). Beryllium's extremely low Poisson's ratio (ν ≈ 0.032) is unusual for a metal and arises from its hexagonal crystal structure and high elastic anisotropy. High specific modulus (E/ρ ≈ 155 GPa·cm³/g) and very high specific heat make it uniquely attractive for lightweight precision structures and thermal management. Maximum service temperature in air limited to ~600 °C by oxidation; higher in vacuum. Shear strength derived from von Mises criterion: UTS (ultimate tensile strength)/√3 = 370/√3 ≈ 214 MPa. Cryogenic table data — coefficient of thermal expansion CTE(T) and specific heat Cp(T), each as a function of temperature T — are from the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Cryogenic Materials Database (nist-cryo-be); NIST polynomial valid 14–284 K only, so cryo entries span −196 to 0 °C. CTE values are mean coefficients from T to 293 K. The 20 °C table entry (10.9 µm/m·K) is the instantaneous CTE at 293 K obtained by evaluating the derivative of the NIST polynomial (dy/dT at T = 293 K); all other table entries are mean coefficients from T to 293 K.

typical_usage: Precision optical mirrors and telescope structures (e.g., James Webb Space Telescope secondary mirror); X-ray windows and monochromators; nuclear reactor moderators and reflectors; aerospace inertial guidance gyroscopes; satellite bus structures and camera mounts where maximum specific stiffness, dimensional stability, and thermal diffusivity are required at minimum mass.
